summary: Describes SPIRITS, a protocol for services that start in the cellular or wireline telephone network and need interactions with the Internet. It lets phone-network events trigger Internet-based services.

eli5.summary: When someone calls your phone, the phone system can tell an internet service, which might pop up a message on your computer.

subtitle: How phone-network events, like an incoming call, are reported to Internet hosts using SIP subscriptions and XML.

tldr.problem: Telephone-network call-processing elements need a standard way to trigger services running on Internet hosts, such as showing a caller's number on a computer.
tldr.mechanism: SPIRITS uses SIP event notification. An Internet host SUBSCRIBEs to events in one of two event packages, and the PSTN side sends NOTIFY requests carrying XML documents of type application/spirits-event+xml.
tldr.outcome: It defines the building blocks (event names, parameters, XML schema, security rules) from which services such as Internet Call Waiting and Internet Caller-ID Delivery can be built.

facts.label: Slow-arming threshold
facts.value: 202 response if arming takes more than 200 ms

sections.title: What SPIRITS Does
sections.content:
SPIRITS (Services in PSTN requesting Internet Services) lets call-processing elements in the telephone network make service requests that are processed on Internet-hosted servers. PSTN here means both wireline and wireless circuit-switched networks. The earlier PINT work (RFC 2848) covered the reverse direction, from the Internet to the PSTN.

In general terms, an Internet host is interested in certain events in the PSTN. When one occurs, the PSTN notifies the host, which can run an appropriate service. Examples named in the abstract are Internet Call Waiting, Internet Caller-ID Delivery and location-based services on the cellular network.

PSTN events fall into two classes: call-related events (setup, teardown and maintenance of a call, either static or dynamic) and non-call-related events such as mobility, registration and de-registration.
sections.eli5: Your phone line and the Internet normally do not talk to each other. SPIRITS gives them a way to pass notes, like "someone is calling you right now".

sections.title: Roles and Architecture
sections.content:
The protocol runs on interfaces B and C of the SPIRITS architecture (RFC 3136). Interface D, between the SPIRITS client and the PSTN's service control, is a matter of local policy and is not discussed in detail.

The protocol is built on SIP and SIP event notification (RFC 3265), and it is a set of two event packages. Because the architecture's names "SPIRITS server" and "SPIRITS client" look reversed, the RFC renames them: the SPIRITS subscriber (the server) is a user agent in the Internet that subscribes to PSTN events, and the SPIRITS notifier (the client) is a user agent in the PSTN that accepts subscriptions and sends notifications.

Subscriptions and notifications are encoded in XML. The requirements and the choice of SIP are described in RFC 3298.
sections.eli5: One side asks "tell me when this happens" and is the subscriber. The other side watches the phone network and is the notifier.

sections.title: The XML Payload
sections.content:
SPIRITS defines the MIME type application/spirits-event+xml, which MUST be in the Content-Type header of SPIRITS requests and responses. The namespace URN is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:spirits-1.0. All subscribers and notifiers MUST support the base schema, and implementations MAY add other XML namespaces for richer events.

The root element is <spirits-event>, which MUST contain at least one <Event> element. Each <Event> has a mandatory type attribute (INDPs for call-related events, userprof for non-call events), a mandatory name attribute (one of the SPIRITS mnemonics) and an optional mode attribute that is N (notification, the default) or R (request).

Inside an INDPs event the elements are <CallingPartyNumber>, <CalledPartyNumber>, <DialledDigits> and <Cause>. A userprof event MUST contain <CalledPartyNumber> and MAY contain <Cell-ID>. A subscriber that does not understand extensions MUST look for the mandatory elements.
sections.eli5: The notes between the two sides are written in a tidy form with labels, like a form with boxes for "who called" and "who was called".

sections.title: Call-Related Events and Detection Points
sections.content:
PSTN Intelligent Network (IN) services run on a call model, a finite state machine made of states called Points In Call (PICs) joined by transitions. Transitions pass through Detection Points (DPs), which hold triggers. When an armed trigger's firing criteria are met, the switch (SSP) sends a message to the control point (SCP).

A TDP is statically armed through service management. An EDP is armed dynamically by the SCP during call processing. Each can be a Request type (-R), where call processing is suspended until a response arrives, or a Notification type (-N), where it carries on.

RFC 3910 lists the IN CS-3 detection points it uses, each with a mnemonic and mandatory parameters. Originating-side examples are OAA, OCI, OA, ONA, OCPB and OD. Terminating-side examples are TA, TNA, TD and TB. For TB (Termination Busy), the Cause parameter is either "Busy" or "Unreachable", which lets a subscriber tell a busy line from a mobile that is not registered.
sections.eli5: A phone call goes through steps, like ringing, answered, hung up. A detection point is a tripwire on one step that rings a bell when someone steps on it.

sections.title: Subscribing to Call Events
sections.content:
Call-related events use the event package spirits-INDPs. Entities set the Event header to it and include the token in Allow-Events. A SUBSCRIBE that establishes a dialog MUST carry a body with the set of DPs, the mode (R or N) and the DP parameters. The notifier MUST authenticate and authorize the request, then arm the DPs through interface D.

If arming may take more than 200 ms, the notifier MUST answer 202 and send a NOTIFY with an empty body and Subscription-State of pending, then another with active once the DPs are armed. When the event fires, the final NOTIFY carries a body and a Subscription-State of terminated with reason fired. The dialog ends there, and un-encountered DPs MUST be disarmed. To keep watching, the subscriber starts a new subscription.

Forking of SUBSCRIBE requests is prohibited, state agents are not used, and the package MUST NOT use URIs to retrieve state. The RFC recommends two or at most three NOTIFY requests per subscription. For statically armed triggers, the PSTN sends a SIP request, typically an INVITE, with a multipart MIME body whose second part holds the SPIRITS information. The Internet Call Waiting walk-through lists seven call dispositions, such as accepting over the PSTN line, accepting over VoIP, rejecting, or forwarding to voice mail.
sections.eli5: You tell the phone system "ring me when Mom calls". It says "okay, ready", and when Mom calls it rings once and the request is finished. For another call you ask again.

sections.title: Non-Call Events in the Cellular Network
sections.content:
Events not tied to a call use the second event package, spirits-user-prof. The required events are location update in the same VLR area (LUSV), location update in a different VLR area (LUDV), IMSI attach (REG), mobile-initiated IMSI detach (UNREGMS) and network-initiated IMSI detach (UNREGNTWK). Subscriptions use CalledPartyNumber, and notifications for the location and attach events also carry a Cell-ID.

Unlike spirits-INDPs, the dialog persists until it expires or the subscriber ends it, because cellular events such as location updates can recur often. The subscriber refreshes with a new SUBSCRIBE, and sends one with Expires of 0 to end it.

To limit traffic, whenever a notifier sends a location update NOTIFY it MUST start a timer Tn of 15 seconds. Any location update NOTIFY that would be sent before Tn expires MUST be discarded.
sections.eli5: This is like asking a friend to text you each time someone moves to a new neighbourhood, but never more than once every 15 seconds so your phone does not buzz nonstop.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC names four security needs from its requirements: authentication, integrity, confidentiality and non-repudiation. It treats interfaces B and C as the ones SPIRITS must secure, assuming the SPIRITS gateway is owned by the same operator as the notifier. Interface D is out of scope.

Because the data is sensitive and may raise privacy concerns, the path between notifier and subscriber should be secured with S/MIME, which encrypts the bodies end to end while routing headers stay in the clear. All SPIRITS endpoints MUST support S/MIME signatures (CMS SignedData) and encryption (CMS EnvelopedData), and all requests and responses between SPIRITS entities MUST be encrypted. TLS or HTTP Digest authentication from SIP (RFC 3261) may also be used.

A notifier MUST authenticate each incoming request, reject the subscription if authentication fails, and check that the subscriber is allowed to receive the events. Requests from the notifier to subscribers MUST also be authenticated, so a malicious party cannot pose as a notifier and hijack a session.
sections.eli5: Calls and locations are private, so the notes are sealed in envelopes and each side must prove who it is before anything is shared.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document asks IANA to register four things: the two SIP event packages (spirits-INDPs and spirits-user-prof), the MIME type application/spirits-event+xml, the namespace URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:spirits-1.0, and the matching XML schema. The base XML schema itself appears in Section 9 of the RFC.
sections.eli5: The names used in the notes were put on an official list so no other system picks the same ones.
